items.prompt:
Create an exactly 30-second 3D animated adventure-comedy in 16:9 horizontal format. Use the attached Milo character sheet as the exact visual reference for Milo. Maintain his identical face, brown eyes, three-feather head tuft, charcoal-grey feathers, cream belly, muted golden neck patches, narrow curved dark beak, long thin flippers, tall pear-shaped proportions, oversized pinkish-grey webbed feet and overall silhouette throughout the entire video. The reference defines Milo’s appearance only.

The story takes place in one continuous sunny autumn forest-edge clearing. An old wild apple tree grows near the upper part of a broad gently sloping grassy hill. One enormous ripe glossy red apple is already lying naturally on the ground beneath the tree before Milo arrives. The apple is approximately the same height as Milo’s torso and head combined. It is far too heavy for him to lift but round enough that he can roll it by pushing. Several meters away lies exactly one naturally detached broad curved slab of tree bark. The bark is approximately twice Milo’s body length, shallowly concave like a natural tray, thick and rigid enough to keep its shape, and wide enough to support the giant apple with Milo sitting behind it. The bark was already detached before the story begins, and Milo never tears it from a tree. A clear grassy trail leads gently downhill from the apple tree. Near the bottom of the hill is one deep pile of loose dry orange and golden autumn leaves positioned directly across the trail. Immediately beyond and slightly beside that leaf pile is Milo’s small round forest shelter entrance built naturally into an earth bank. The entrance is visibly smaller than the giant apple. Keep the apple tree uphill and the shelter downhill for the entire video.

Use a premium photorealistic 3D CGI animated feature-film aesthetic with highly detailed soft penguin feathers, realistic bark, glossy apple skin, dry autumn leaves, lush vegetation, expressive character animation, cinematic warm daylight, vibrant natural colors and exaggerated physical-comedy timing. Maintain realistic gravity, friction, momentum, weight, collisions and object support underneath the stylized animation. Use warm sunny autumn daylight throughout with natural cinematic depth of field. There is no dialogue, no text, no subtitles, no logos, no HUD and no additional characters.

From 0:00 to 0:02, open with a wide low tracking shot. Milo suddenly bursts through a patch of low autumn plants and runs into the sunny clearing. His oversized webbed feet rapidly slap against the grass, his long flippers swing beside him and his three-feather tuft bounces slightly. Milo suddenly stops when he sees the enormous glossy red apple beneath the old tree. Warm sunlight reflects from its surface. Milo’s eyes widen, his beak opens slightly and his expression immediately becomes excited.

From 0:02 to 0:04, move into a medium frontal shot beside the apple. Milo inspects the enormous fruit, then crouches beside its lowest accessible side. He slides both long flippers underneath it as far as physically possible, bends his knees and tries to lift. The apple does not move. Milo strains harder while his oversized webbed feet begin slipping slightly backward through the grass, but the apple remains fully supported by the ground.

From 0:04 to 0:06, use a wide side shot. Milo makes one final enormous lifting effort. His flippers lose their grip against the smooth apple and he falls backward onto the grass. The apple stays completely stationary. Milo lies dazed for a brief moment, raises his head, looks at the apple and then scans the clearing. His eyes stop on the broad curved piece of detached bark lying nearby. He looks at the bark, then at the apple, then back at the bark. His expression changes as he gets an idea.

From 0:06 to 0:08, use a wide side tracking shot that clearly shows Milo’s full body, both webbed feet and the entire bark slab at the same time. Milo quickly runs to one narrow end of the bark and remains completely standing on the grass. He does not sit, stand, kneel or ride on the bark. Milo faces the bark, bends forward and grips the narrow end using both long flippers. Both oversized webbed feet stay firmly on the ground. Milo begins walking backward toward the apple, stepping backward with one foot and then the other. His feet press against the grass and provide the traction that moves his body backward. Because both flippers are gripping the bark, his backward movement pulls the bark across the ground toward him. Most of the bark remains continuously supported by and in contact with the grass. The bark never moves underneath Milo and Milo’s body never rests on it. He drags it all the way to the giant apple and releases it.

From 0:08 to 0:11, use one clear wide side shot showing Milo, the complete apple and the entire bark slab. Milo positions the bark flat on the grass immediately downhill from the apple with its shallow concave surface facing upward. One end lies close to the fruit. Milo walks around to the uphill side of the apple, places both flippers against it and pushes. His webbed feet remain firmly planted on the ground. The apple slowly rotates forward, first one quarter turn and then another, until it rolls directly onto the center of the curved bark slab. Milo immediately stops pushing. The apple settles naturally into the shallow concave center while the bark remains fully supported by the ground.

From 0:11 to 0:13.5, show a wide lateral view. Milo walks behind the loaded bark sled and places both long flippers firmly against its rear edge while both feet remain completely on the grass. He leans his pear-shaped body forward and pushes. The bark begins scraping slowly across the nearly flat ground. His feet visibly push backward against the grass with every step. Milo remains on the ground and does not ride the bark yet. The apple remains nested in the center and moves together with the bark as one loaded sled.

From 0:13.5 to 0:15.5, use a wide side shot clearly showing the ground transitioning from almost flat grass into a gentle downhill trail. Milo continues pushing from behind. The front half of the loaded bark reaches the downward slope. As more of the sled moves onto the incline, gravity begins pulling it forward. Milo notices that it is becoming easier to push. The bark gradually starts moving slightly faster than Milo’s walking pace. Milo removes his flippers from the rear edge and begins running directly behind it.

From 0:15.5 to 0:18, use a dynamic side tracking shot. The loaded bark continues sliding downhill at a moderate speed because of gravity. Milo runs behind it using his oversized webbed feet. He catches up while the sled is still moving slowly enough to board safely. Milo reaches forward and places both flippers over the rear side edges of the bark. He takes two quick running steps, places one webbed foot onto the rear portion of the bark, then the second foot, and immediately lowers his body. Milo sits securely behind the giant apple and grips the bark edges with both flippers. This is the first time in the entire video that Milo sits or rides on the bark.

From 0:18 to 0:21, use a wide cinematic tracking shot moving alongside the trail. The loaded bark sled continues sliding naturally down the gentle hill. Dry leaves scatter slightly underneath the front and side edges. The trail remains completely clear. The bark stays continuously in contact with the ground. The apple remains seated securely in the shallow concave center and does not roll independently. Milo sits directly behind it. At first he looks nervous and grips the bark tightly. After a moment, he realizes the ride is stable. His expression slowly changes from concern to excitement and a delighted smile appears.

From 0:21 to 0:23.5, move into a closer side tracking shot. The downhill trail becomes slightly steeper but remains smooth and safe, causing gravity to moderately increase the sled’s speed. Milo continues gripping the bark edges. His charcoal-grey feathers and three-feather tuft move gently in the rushing air. He looks forward and realizes everything appears under control. His confidence grows. Milo straightens his upper body slightly while remaining securely seated, pushes his chest forward and smiles proudly as though the entire ride was planned.

From 0:23.5 to 0:25.5, use a front-facing tracking shot moving backward downhill. Milo continues riding proudly behind the giant apple. He looks past the fruit toward the bottom of the hill. Camera pulls slightly wider and reveals the enormous deep pile of orange and golden autumn leaves directly across the trail. Beyond and slightly beside the pile is Milo’s small shelter entrance. Milo initially smiles when he sees home, but then notices how quickly the leaf pile is approaching. His expression changes immediately and he grips both sides of the bark more tightly.

From 0:25.5 to 0:27, use one uninterrupted wide side-profile shot. The loaded bark sled enters the deep pile of loose dry autumn leaves. The leaves create strong resistance and friction against the bark, causing the sled to rapidly but smoothly lose speed. A large soft burst of orange and golden leaves sprays outward. The bark remains flat against the ground and never flips. The giant apple stays inside the shallow center and does not launch forward. Milo naturally leans forward because of the deceleration but remains seated safely behind the apple. The sled comes to a complete stop inside the soft leaf pile. Nothing breaks.

From 0:27 to 0:28.5, use a medium shot beside the leaf pile. Milo climbs carefully off the stopped bark sled and steps onto the grass. He looks at the giant apple, then turns toward his nearby shelter entrance. His proud smile returns. Milo positions himself behind the apple, places both flippers against it and pushes. The apple rolls slowly off the bark with one controlled rotation and then another. Milo continues walking behind it and pushing it across the short flat patch of ground toward the shelter.

From 0:28.5 to 0:30, finish with a static frontal comedy shot facing the shelter entrance. The enormous red apple rolls directly toward the small round doorway. Its diameter is clearly larger than the opening. The curved sides of the apple contact the earth around both sides of the entrance and it stops with a low soft thud. Milo continues pushing for one brief moment but nothing moves. He stops, looks at the shelter entrance, looks at the enormous apple, looks back at the entrance, then slowly looks at the apple again. After one small silent beat, Milo calmly walks around the side of the fruit, sits comfortably on the grass, leans toward the apple and takes one enormous satisfied bite. His eyes close happily and he smiles. Cut to black.

Maintain strict Milo consistency throughout all 30 seconds. Never alter his facial structure, brown eyes, three-feather tuft, charcoal-grey feathers, cream belly, muted golden neck patches, dark curved beak, long thin flippers, oversized pinkish-grey webbed feet, pear-shaped body or overall silhouette.

There is exactly one giant red apple. It begins resting on the ground beneath the apple tree and remains the exact same fruit throughout the entire video. It never falls from the tree, teleports, duplicates or changes size. There is exactly one curved bark slab. It begins lying naturally on the grass and Milo physically moves it. The bark never moves by itself before Milo pushes it onto the visible downhill slope. It never floats, flies, flips, changes size, changes shape or behaves like fabric.

Before 0:15.5, Milo must never sit, stand, kneel, balance or ride on the bark. During the 0:06 to 0:08 dragging action, Milo remains entirely on the grass. Both webbed feet must remain clearly visible on the ground while he walks backward and pulls the bark using both flippers. Never depict Milo sitting on the same bark that he is trying to drag. During the apple-loading and pushing sequence, Milo also remains entirely on the ground. Milo boards the bark for the first time only from 0:15.5 onward after gravity has already started moving the loaded sled downhill.

When the apple is on the bark, its full weight remains physically supported by the concave bark surface. The apple never hovers or balances on invisible support. During the downhill ride, the apple stays in direct contact with the bark and does not independently roll ahead or backward. The loaded sled moves slowly across flat ground only while Milo physically pushes it. Continued motion and acceleration occur only once the sled reaches the visible downhill slope and gravity acts on it.

The leaf pile is already present before Milo reaches it and contains only loose dry leaves. There are no hidden rocks, logs or hard objects inside. The increasing friction and resistance of the leaves gradually stop the sled. Milo does not fly out, the bark does not flip and the apple does not launch forward.

The shelter entrance remains exactly the same size throughout the video and the apple remains exactly the same size. The ending works only because the apple was already wider than the doorway. The doorway never shrinks and the apple never grows.

Maintain one continuous uphill-to-downhill geography. The apple tree remains uphill and the shelter remains downhill. Do not mirror or reverse the environment between shots. Once Milo passes a location, it remains geographically behind him. No teleportation, object duplication, object regeneration, invisible supports, spontaneous acceleration, unexplained movement, additional animals or humans.

Use readable cinematic framing throughout. Use wide lateral views whenever physical cause and effect matters. During the bark-dragging sequence, keep Milo’s full body, both webbed feet and the entire bark visible at the same time. During the apple-loading action, clearly show the apple physically rolling onto the bark. During the loaded-sled push, clearly show Milo behind the bark with both feet on the ground. Clearly reveal the terrain becoming downhill before the sled begins moving independently. During boarding, show Milo running behind the sled and physically stepping onto it without hiding the transition. Keep the downhill direction consistent and never use camera rotation to fake sled movement.

Use a playful adventurous orchestral score throughout. Include rapid webbed-foot footsteps during Milo’s opening run, natural autumn forest ambience, soft wind through leaves, comedic effort sounds while he tries lifting the apple, a soft thump when he falls backward, realistic bark scraping over grass as he drags it, clear webbed footsteps during the dragging action, a low rolling sound as the apple moves onto the bark, heavier scraping as he pushes the loaded sled and gradually more adventurous music when the sled reaches the slope. Add rhythmic dry-leaf and bark-sliding sounds during the downhill ride, light wind rush as the speed increases and a triumphant musical feeling as Milo becomes confident. When the leaf pile appears, shift briefly into playful tension. Use a large soft rush and poof as the sled enters the leaves, followed by falling and settling leaf sounds. Add soft apple-rolling sounds near the shelter, a low thud when the apple contacts the doorway, a tiny pushing effort sound, then brief silence as Milo realizes the problem. Finish with one crisp apple bite and one tiny satisfied orchestral note before cutting to black.

Shallow depth of field, soft bokeh from sunlight hitting metal bleacher rails, handheld documentary-style camera with gentle drift, 24fps film grain, warm orange-and-teal color grade, lens flares from low sun.

**Shot 1 (0–5s):** Close-mid shot of a teenage girl with soft blonde hair pulled into a messy bun, wearing an off-shoulder cream sweater over a black tank top. She sits on metal bleachers scrolling intently on her phone. Beside her, a teenage boy in a light blue oversized hoodie with shaggy brown hair leans in close over her shoulder, peering at the screen with mild curiosity. Soft rim lighting from the setting sun behind them, blurred silver bleacher rows in the background, a few autumn leaves scattered on the seats.

**Shot 2 (5–9s):** Sudden jump cut — a burst of red smoke or colored powder explodes into frame, enveloping a small group of three teens sitting further down the bleachers. They flinch back in surprise, hands raised defensively to shield their faces, hair and loose strands whipped by the gust of the blast. Golden sunlight scatters through the red haze creating a hazy, dreamlike, slightly chaotic visual. Quick, reactive camera shake sells the surprise.

**Shot 3 (9–14s):** Intimate close-up portrait of a different girl — wavy, sunlit flyaway hair, delicate gold hoop earrings and a thin gold necklace, wearing a white knitted top. She looks down at her phone with a quiet, pensive, slightly worried expression, warm backlight haloing her hair, skin tones glowing in the low sun. The mood shifts from chaos to a quieter, tense beat.

**Shot 4 (14–20s):** Low-angle wide shot looking straight up at a bright yellow steel goalpost crossbar cutting diagonally across a clear, deep-blue late-afternoon sky. Below it, three teenagers stand on the field looking upward with concern and frustration — one boy in a grey hoodie with a black backpack reaches up and starts climbing the vertical post, straining to reach something lodged at the top. Two girls stand nearby, one with long brown hair looking up anxiously, the other in a navy striped sweater raising both hands toward the sky in a pleading/frustrated gesture. Their phones are visibly stuck on top of the crossbar. Blurred autumn-orange treeline and stadium floodlight tower visible at the edges of frame.

**Overall mood/theme:** "Messing with Amelia" backfires — a lighthearted teen revenge-prank narrative where the antagonist group's phones end up stranded on the stadium goalpost, and they're now desperately trying to climb up and fetch them. Comedic-ironic, youthful, slightly cinematic-trailer energy. Aspect ratio 1080x608, widescreen cinematic crop, subtle ambient wind/rustle sound design implied, no dialogue — purely visual storytelling with expressive reactions.

Gus climbs into the cart and Benny pushes him faster and faster down the aisle, until a police officer standing ahead orders them to stop. Benny can't stop the cart in time and it crashes into the officer. The friends scramble up and run away laughing while the angry officer shouts after them. Duration: 20 seconds. . Starts with a relatable hook and ends on a laughing escape.

Rich colorful product shelves, warm cream floor tiles with soft green accents. Playful, energetic, fast comic timing. Big expressive eyes, rubbery stretchy motion, exaggerated reactions. He turns slowly to Benny and says: "Are you thinking what I am thinking?" Benny looks at him for a beat, then grins just as excitedly.
→ Camera: quick whip-pan to Gus, a tight close-up (50mm feel) on his lit-up eyes and grin, then a two-shot as he turns to Benny, and a push-in on Benny's growing grin.

Scene 3, 5–11s, The Cart Ride: Gus climbs onto the cart and sits in the child seat at the back, legs dangling, arms in the air. Benny grips the red handle and starts pushing him faster through the aisle. They burst into laughter. They swap places, taking turns pushing and riding, while the cart speeds down the aisle past shelves and product displays. Gus shouts: "FASTER! FASTER!" Benny laughs wildly and runs even faster.
→ Camera: low-angle front-facing dolly-back shot, keeping the cart and both friends in frame as they speed toward the camera. Then a side tracking shot at running speed with motion blur on the shelves, a close-up on Gus's wind-blown ginger hair and open-mouthed laugh, and a quick cut to Benny's wheels-and-sneakers pounding the floor.

Scene 4, 11–14s, Officer Ahead: close-up on the police officer standing in the aisle ahead, his back half-turned, until the noise makes him turn. His eyes widen as he sees the cart racing toward him. Behind them, the officer struggles to stand, picks his cap up, points furiously at them and shouts: "YOU TWO! COME BACK HERE!" [VFX]

[CAMERA AND PERFORMANCE]

Lens and movement: natural 35mm and 50mm feel, shallow depth of field on faces, smooth gimbal tracking, deliberate push-ins for reactions, a crash zoom only on the officer, and a handheld feel only during the chase and escape.
Benny: bored, then excited, then panicked, then guilty and laughing.
Gus: bored, then mischievous, then wildly joyful, then dazed, then laughing.
Officer: stern and heavy, furious, comically flustered.

[AUDIO]
Music: playful upbeat comedic track. A slow, lazy shuffle with a single bored tuba and light pizzicato in Scene 1, a quick cheeky "idea" sting in Scene 2, a fast, bouncy, fun chase groove (quirky percussion, slide whistle, bouncy bass) in Scene 3, a sudden tense drum-roll stop in Scene 4, a big cartoon crash hit with a silence beat in Scene 5, then a fast, frantic, sneaky-escape theme in Scene 6. Music ducks under dialogue.

Dialogue (English, short and clear): Benny: "Man, this is boring." Gus: "Are you thinking what I am thinking?" Gus: "FASTER! FASTER!" Police Officer: "HEY! STOP RIGHT THERE!" Police Officer: "YOU TWO! COME BACK HERE!" Plus laughter, screams and groans.
Voices: Benny's deep, warm voice, Gus's light, excitable voice, and the officer's low, gruff, angry voice.
Ambience: a busy, echoey mall with soft speaker hum.
Subtitles: off.

[KEEP CONSISTENT]
Same Gus (@image4), Benny (@image5), officer (@image1), cart (@image2) and mall (@image3) in every shot. Characters' clothes and proportions never change. The cart keeps its red handle. The officer's cap and badge stay consistent. Bright, warm lighting throughout. Smooth, continuous motion between scenes.

items.prompt:
Create an exactly 30-second vertical 9:16 premium 3D animated comedy short. Use the attached Nibs character sheet as the exact visual reference for Nibs. Maintain his identical face, amber-brown eyes, oversized cream front teeth, dark chocolate-brown fur, cream muzzle and chest, compact body proportions, short legs, front paws and large flat beaver tail throughout every frame. The reference defines Nibs’ appearance only. If a storyboard board is also provided, use it only as a sequence and composition guide. One rooted tree stump and one large immovable rock sit approximately one meter apart. Both ends of the branch are firmly supported, so the branch cannot roll, fall, rotate, bend or move. This branch already exists in this stable position before the story begins. Several meters away on the grass lies exactly one enormous detached green forest leaf. The leaf is already naturally detached before the story begins. Nibs never tears it from a plant. The leaf has one long green stem, one thick central midrib and one broad flexible leaf blade. The leaf is approximately twice Nibs’ body length but lightweight enough for him to drag and manipulate with both front paws. It is flexible like a large real leaf but does not behave like cloth, rubber or paper.
The core story is simple. Nibs is proudly organizing his dry acorn stash when rain begins. He tries to protect the acorns using his own body, then notices the giant detached leaf. Nibs drags the leaf toward the stash and uses the already-fixed horizontal branch as a simple roof ridge. He places the leaf’s thick central midrib across the top of the branch so the broad leaf blade naturally drapes down on both sides. The leaf creates a tiny tent-like rain cover over the acorns. The shelter works perfectly. Rain runs down the outside of the leaf and the acorns remain dry. Nibs becomes extremely proud of his engineering, then tries to crawl underneath and discovers that he made the shelter only large enough for the acorns. There is no room for him. Nibs ends up sitting outside in the rain while his stash remains perfectly dry. In the final moment he reaches inside, takes one dry acorn and proudly nods as if the design was still a complete success.
Use a premium realistic 3D CGI animated-feature aesthetic with highly detailed soft beaver fur, realistic wet grass, natural bark, damp soil, detailed acorn surfaces, realistic leaf veins, soft rain, cinematic overcast daylight and expressive but physically controlled character animation. Keep the environment lush, natural and visually appealing. The rain should create small visible droplets and subtle wetness on exposed surfaces, but do not create flooding, strong wind, lightning, thunder, violent weather or rapidly growing puddles. Every major movement must have a visible physical cause.
From 0:00 to 0:02, open with a medium-low cinematic shot of Nibs crouched happily beside his compact pile of dry acorns beneath the fixed horizontal branch. He carefully adjusts one acorn with both front paws and looks proudly at the neat pile. One large raindrop falls vertically from above and lands directly on the top of Nibs’ nose. Nibs freezes. His eyes slowly cross toward the droplet. He looks upward.
From 0:02 to 0:04, additional raindrops begin falling around him. The rain changes from isolated drops into a gentle steady shower. Nibs looks immediately toward the acorn pile. His large flat tail remains permanently attached behind him and rests naturally on the ground. Nibs does not remove or use his tail as an umbrella.
From 0:04 to 0:06, Nibs realizes his body cannot cover the entire pile. He raises his head and scans the nearby clearing. His eyes stop on the single enormous detached green leaf lying flat on the grass several meters away. The leaf remains motionless except for small natural rain impacts.
